newsitem.title: USA: Price sees REIT stocks as too high.
newsitem.headline: Price sees REIT stocks as too high.

text.p: Mutual fund executive Michael Price said on Tuesday he believes that real estate investment trust stocks are valued too highly, but he likes HMO, defense and some money center bank stocks.
Price, chairman and president of Mutual Series Fund Inc, a mutual fund company, spoke at the Sixth Annual Graham and Dodd Breakfast sponsored by Columbia University Business School.
Price said that in July his funds were buyers of HMOs, and he continues to hold a big stake in Chase Manhattan Corp.
He said REIT stocks are 30-40 percent above where they should be selling.
Price believes the U.S. stock market is "toppy." He said: "Ben Graham said you should buy common stocks like groceries, not like perfumes. The market is perfumey."
He referred to the late Columbia business professor Benjamin Graham, who is known on Wall Street for his theories in value investing.
Price said it is harder in today's market to find undervalued common stocks, and he often takes alternate routes, such as buying into rights offerings by corporations.
He said he sees spinoffs and bankruptcies as good ways to find undervalued securities.
"We like to play consolidation industries," Price said.

Price was asked how he values technology shares. He said that unlike other other industries, valuing the prospects for future product revenues is risker, and he tends to be conservative when assigning values and after factoring in cash and other hard assets. He did not mention any stocks he likes.
Last year, Price, who was a big holder in Chase before it merged with Chemical Bank, pressured Chase management to increase the share price.
Many believe that it was his pressure that forced Chase managers to make a deal with Chemical last year. The two banks completed their merger this year.
At the breakfast, Price said he never intended to tell managers how to run their business but wanted them to be responsible to shareholders and improve the share price.
He said that remains his philosophy.

Price said his Mutual Shares fund, with assets of about $5 billion, has about 21 percent in cash currently -- significantly higher than the average U.S. equity fund, which has about 7.2 percent in cash, according to Lipper Analytical Services.
Price said he is currently preferring short-term Treasuries and is shying away from 30-year bonds.
